title: Consent-header-aware EU routing with tenant allow/deny and pseudonymization fallback
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem: some customers require all inference that originates from EU-scoped accounts or includes an explicit residency consent header (X-Residence: EU) to be served from EU-hosted model variants. Conversely, other customers are blocked from EU routing via denylist. We need a deterministic, auditable router that resolves precedence between per-tenant residency flags, request-level consent headers, and customer allowlists/denylists. When strict EU routing cannot be satisfied (no capacity, policy conflict), the system should optionally apply a pseudonymization preprocessor and route to an approved non-EU tier with a soft-deny signal recorded. Goal: implement a policy-driven routing adaptor that supports header-driven consent, tenant-level controls, precedence rules, fallback pseudonymization, and full audit trails for compliance teams.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Router consults tenant config and X-Residence header and makes routing decision deterministically (same inputs => same route).
2) Priority order: tenant-blocklist deny > tenant-residency-enforce > request-residency-header > tenant-allowlist override. Documentable and tested.

3) If tenant requires EU-only and no EU capacity is available, route to fallback that applies pseudonymization and mark request as 'soft-deny' in audit logs; do not return inference output until pseudonymization step completes.
4) All routing decisions emit standardized telemetry: route_outcome, decision_path, tenant_id, model_variant, capacity_zone, and policy_version.
5) Console UI exposes per-tenant residency flags and allow/deny lists and a toggle for pseudonymization fallback; changes are versioned and reflected within 30s.
6) Security review completed and KMS/HSM policy annotated for any pseudonymized payloads that get stored in transient caches.
7) End-to-end tests cover: header-only requests, tenant-only flags, conflicting configs, capacity-failure fallback, and audit log verification.
8) Rollout gated behind feature-flag with canary at 5% of EU traffic and quick rollback path.
9) Documentation published: routing precedence doc, API contract for X-Residence header, and customer-facing KB entry.
10) No regressions in latency p50/p95 beyond 5ms for routing decision path in normal flows.
11) Metrics for misroutes (requests that violate tenant policy) must be < 0.01% after canary and < 0.001% in GA.
12) Update allowed: admin users can add/remove tenants from allow/deny lists and see history in audit logs.
13) Unit and integration tests added to routing-service test-suite; CI must pass before merge.
technical_design: Overview: Introduce a Policy Decision Layer (PDL) within route-decider that evaluates a compact policy tree: 1) tenant denylist, 2) tenant residency_enforce flag, 3) request X-Residence header, 4) tenant allowlist. Each decision is tagged with policy_version. Implementation components: - tenant-config-store (existing Redis+Postgres mix) extended with 'residency_mode' {off,enforce,allowlist-only,block} and 'pseudonymize_on_fallback' boolean; - request-interceptor middleware (SDK + REST ingress) that normalizes X-Residence and attaches resolved identity metadata; - route-decider PDL microservice returns: target_region, model_variant, fallback_action (none|pseudonymize|reject), decision_path string; - egress-enforcer ensures selected target_region is compatible with model variant; - audit-log writer appends an immutable event to compliance-log topic (encrypted). Pseudonymizer: lightweight preprocessor that strips or hashes PII fields per tenant policy using per-tenant salt from KMS. Policy precedence: denylist MUST win; enforce flag means only EU routes allowed; header is respected only if tenant has not explicitly denied/enforced contradictory policy; allowlist can be used to explicitly force EU route for specific tenants. Dataflow: request -> interceptor -> PDL -> model router -> egress. All decisions tagged with policy_version and emitted to tracing and metrics.

rollout_plan: Create feature flag 'eu_consent_routing_v1' and gate all new PDL code behind it.
Deploy PDL and pseudonymizer to canary cluster in eu-west-1 with feature flag off by default.
Enable flag for internal test tenants and run end-to-end tests for 48 hours.
Canary 1: enable 5% of EU traffic for non-production tenants; monitor misroutes, latency, and audit logs.
Canary 2: expand to 20% EU traffic and include a subset of paying customers with consent to test scale.
GA: enable for all tenants with default 'off' so customers must opt-in or be changed via Console.
Provide rollback steps: disable feature flag -> wait 30s -> verify decision path reverted and purge any transient pseudonymized caches.
Coordinate with Support/Account teams for customers that need immediate changes; provide migration window.
Post-GA: 30-day monitoring period with weekly compliance reviews.
monitoring_and_alerting: routing.misroute.count - alert if > 0.01% of routed requests in canary or > 0.001% in GA over 10m.
routing.decision_latency.p95 - alert if increases by > 10ms relative to baseline.
pseudonymizer.errors - alert and circuit-break fallback to reject mode for affected tenant until resolved.
capacity.europe.available_slots - used by route-decider to decide fallback; alert if < 5% for > 5m.
console.config-change - audit trail and signal for any direct edits to tenant allow/deny lists.
runbook: If misroute spike detected: 1) Check routing.decision_path samples in traces to identify why tenant was routed incorrectly.
2) Verify tenant-config for deny/enforce flags and policy_version; if corrupted, revert to previous config version via console.
3) If due to EU capacity shortage, verify capacity.europe.available_slots and trigger emergency allocation per dedicated capacity playbook.
4) If pseudonymizer failures occur, enable 'reject_on_pseudonymize_failure' for affected tenants and notify Security/Compliance.
5) For audit-log write failures, escalate to infra and enable synchronous fallback that writes to durable S3 with server-side encryption until Kafka is healthy.
6) Communicate to affected customers with templated incident message and remediation ETA.
notes: Trade-off: pseudonymization reduces fidelity; product needs to own customer-facing messaging when fallback occurs.
We considered a strict-reject fallback but chose pseudonymization to reduce customer-visible failures for PLG users.
Policy precedence ordering was chosen to make denylist absolute for obvious compliance reasons; allowlist is treated as an override only when not conflicting.
We must ensure per-tenant salt rotation strategy with KMS to avoid replayable pseudonyms; security to advise.
Potential future: support country-level granularity (e.g., DE-only) and per-route policies.
